lead: The z-transform turns a difference equation into algebra. For zero initial conditions the ratio H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) is the transfer function, and the impulse response h[n] is its inverse transform. The region of convergence (ROC) decides causality and BIBO stability. Setting z = e<sup>jω</sup> gives the frequency response, so one function gives a digital filter's gain and phase. Engineers use this before coding an ECG noise filter, an audio equaliser or a motor controller: poles near the unit circle warn of slow ringing.
prereq: You need: the z-transform and ROC, inverse z-transform, and difference equations, causality and BIBO stability from the earlier topics on discrete-time systems.

blocks.text: A discrete-time LTI system obeys Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>N</sup> a<sub>k</sub> y[n-k] = Σ<sub>k=0</sub><sup>M</sup> b<sub>k</sub> x[n-k]. The a<sub>k</sub> and b<sub>k</sub> are real constants; a<sub>0</sub> is usually 1. Take the two-sided z-transform with zero initial conditions. A shift by k multiplies a transform by z<sup>−k</sup>, so the equation becomes Σ a<sub>k</sub> z<sup>−k</sup>Y(z)=Σ b<sub>k</sub> z<sup>−k</sup>X(z).
Y(z) and X(z) are z-transforms of output and input; a<sub>k</sub>, b<sub>k</sub> are real coefficients; M and N are non-negative integers; H(z) is the transfer function.

The denominator roots are poles; numerator roots are zeros. The impulse response is h[n]=Z<sup>−1</sup>{H(z)}, because x[n]=δ[n] gives X(z)=1 and Y(z)=H(z). Always quote the ROC with H(z). The ROC of Y(z) is at least the intersection of the ROCs of X(z) and H(z), and can be larger if poles and zeros cancel. The ROC of H(z) itself is fixed by its own poles — for example |z| > r for a causal system. For y[n] − 0.5y[n−1] = x[n], H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5z<sup>−1</sup>), pole z = 0.5.

Causality means h[n] = 0 for n < 0. For a causal rational H(z) the ROC is |z| > r, where r is the largest pole magnitude; it includes z = ∞ when H(∞) is finite. BIBO stability means every bounded input gives a bounded output. It holds when Σ|h[n]|<∞, which for rational H(z) is exactly when the ROC contains the unit circle |z|=1.

For a causal system the ROC is |z|>r. Stability then needs r<1, so every pole lies strictly inside the unit circle. A pole at 0.5 is stable; a pole at 1.2 is causal but unstable. A stable non-causal system can have an annular ROC such as 0.5<|z|<2 that contains |z|=1. Read stability from the ROC, not from poles alone.

The same H(z) with |z|>0.5 gives h[n]=(0.5)<sup>n</sup>u[n], causal and stable. With |z| < 0.5 the algebra gives h[n] = −(0.5)<sup>n</sup>u[−n−1], non-causal and unstable because |z| = 1 is outside the ROC.

sections.h3: Frequency response and sinusoidal steady state

blocks.text: If the ROC contains |z|=1, put z=e<sup>jω</sup>. H(e<sup>jω</sup>) is the frequency response; ω is in radians per sample and the response repeats every 2π. |H(e<sup>jω</sup>)| is gain, ∠H(e<sup>jω</sup>) is phase in radians. For H(z)=1/(1−a z<sup>−1</sup>), |H(e<sup>jω</sup>)|=1/√(1+a²−2a cos ω). A pole at a=0.9 gives gain 10 at ω=0; a=0.5 gives gain 2. The nearer pole gives a sharper low-pass peak.
A is input amplitude; ω₀ is input frequency in rad/sample; φ is input phase in radians; y<sub>ss</sub> is the steady-state output; the system must be stable.
For a=0.5 and ω0=π/3, |H|=1/√(1.25−cos(π/3))≈1.1547 and ∠H=−π/6. Thus x[n]=3 cos(πn/3) gives y<sub>ss</sub>[n]≈3.464 cos(πn/3−π/6).

Initial conditions use the one-sided transform Y⁺(z)=Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>∞</sup> y[n]z<sup>−n</sup>. Shifts: y[n−1]→z<sup>−1</sup>Y⁺(z)+y[−1]; y[n−2]→z<sup>−2</sup>Y⁺(z)+z<sup>−1</sup>y[−1]+y[−2]. Substitute y[−1], y[−2] before solving.

For y[n]−0.5y[n−1]=x[n] with y[−1]=2, Y⁺(z)−0.5(z<sup>−1</sup>Y⁺(z)+2)=X(z). So Y⁺(z)=[X(z)+1]/(1−0.5z<sup>−1</sup>). The term 1/(1−0.5z<sup>−1</sup>) is the zero-input response, (0.5)<sup>n</sup>u[n]; X(z)/(1−0.5z<sup>−1</sup>) is the zero-state response. With x[n]=u[n], inverting gives (2−(0.5)<sup>n</sup>)u[n] + (0.5)<sup>n</sup>u[n] = 2u[n].

An inverse system has H<sub>i</sub>(z)=1/H(z). Its poles are zeros of H(z). If H(z)=(1−2z<sup>−1</sup>)/(1−0.5z<sup>−1</sup>), H is stable (pole 0.5) but the causal inverse has a pole at 2, so it is unstable. Only a few syllabi list deconvolution.

figure.caption: H(z) = z/(z − 0.5) has a zero at 0 and a pole at 0.5; the causal ROC |z| > 0.5 contains the unit circle, so the system is stable. Its step response climbs 1, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, … to the final value 2.

examples.question: A system obeys y[n] − 0.5 y[n-1] = x[n] with zero initial conditions. Find H(z) and its ROC, decide causality and stability, give h[n], and find the step response for x[n] = u[n].
steps: Take the z-transform with zero initial conditions: Y(z) − 0.5z⁻¹Y(z) = X(z).
Set the denominator to zero: 1 − 0.5z⁻¹ = 0 gives pole z = 0.5.
For a causal impulse response the ROC is the exterior of the pole circle: |z| > 0.5.
The unit circle |z| = 1 lies inside |z| > 0.5, so the system is causal and BIBO stable.
The inverse transform of H(z) with ROC |z| > 0.5 is h[n] = (0.5)<sup>n</sup> u[n].
Inverse transform: y[n] = (2 − (0.5)<sup>n</sup>)u[n]. Then y[0] = 1, y[1] = 1.5, y[2] = 1.75, and the final value is 2 (also lim<sub>z→1</sub>(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)Y(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2).
examples.answer: H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹), ROC |z| > 0.5, causal and BIBO stable, h[n] = (0.5)<sup>n</sup> u[n], and the step response is y[n] = (2 − (0.5)<sup>n</sup>)u[n] with steady-state value 2.
examples.check:
a = 0.5
pole = a
steady = 1 / (1 - a)
y0 = steady - a**0
y1 = steady - a**1
y2 = steady - a**2
print(pole)
print(steady)
print(y0)
print(y1)
print(y2)

traps: Reading stability from pole positions alone: stability means the ROC contains |z|=1; for a causal system every pole must be strictly inside the unit circle.
Marking a causal system stable when a pole sits exactly on |z|=1. The ROC then starts at that circle and does not contain it, so BIBO stability fails.
Using H(e<sup>jω</sup>) when the ROC excludes the unit circle. The algebra still evaluates, but it is not a steady-state frequency response.
Dropping the y[−1] term in one-sided transforms. y[n−1] becomes z⁻¹Y⁺(z)+y[−1], not just z⁻¹Y⁺(z).
Assuming 1/H(z) is stable because H(z) is. Zeros of H outside the unit circle become unstable poles of the causal inverse.

quiz.q: Define H(z) for a difference-equation system with zero initial conditions.
quiz.a: H(z) = Y(z)/X(z), the ratio of the output z-transform to the input z-transform, with zero initial conditions.

quiz.q: State the ROC shape for a causal rational H(z).
quiz.a: The ROC is the exterior of a circle, |z| > r, where r is the largest pole magnitude; it includes z = ∞ when H(∞) is finite.

quiz.q: Why can the same H(z) formula describe a stable and an unstable system?
quiz.a: The algebra H(z) does not fix the ROC. Different ROCs give different impulse responses; stability depends on whether the ROC contains |z| = 1.

quiz.q: For y[n] − 0.8y[n-1] = x[n] with zero initial conditions, find H(z), the pole, the ROC, and stability.
quiz.a: H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.8z⁻¹). Pole z = 0.8. Causal ROC |z| > 0.8. The unit circle is inside the ROC, so the system is BIBO stable.

quiz.q: For H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹) and x[n] = 3cos(πn/3), find the steady-state amplitude and phase.
A causal system has a pole at 1.1. Can it be BIBO stable? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Causality gives ROC |z| > 1.1, which does not contain |z| = 1, so the impulse response is not absolutely summable.

quiz.q: H(z) has pole 0.4 and zero 2.5. H is causal and stable. Is the causal inverse stable?
quiz.a: No. The causal inverse 1/H(z) has a pole at 2.5, outside the unit circle, so its ROC |z| > 2.5 does not contain |z| = 1.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice H(z) is implemented as a difference equation or as a cascade of second-order sections; poles near the unit circle give low damping and long settling. Digital control uses the same poles inside the unit circle for stability, and audio filters place poles and zeros to shape gain. Search for 'digital filter design poles zeros', 'bilinear transform', and 'adaptive notch filter'. Deconvolution appears in channel equalisation and image restoration.
